name: Dark Slate Grey
lede: Dark Slate Grey is the web's `darkslategray`, a deep green-teal grey inherited from a 1980s Unix color list, and not, despite its name, a darker version of slate grey.

sections.title: From a Unix file to every browser
sections.body:
The name comes from `rgb.txt`, the list of named colors that shipped with the X Window System, first with X10 Release 3 in June 1986 [1]. Who wrote the original list is not recorded [2]. The big expansion came with X11 Release 4 in January 1989, when Paul Raveling added colors based on Sinclair Paints samples and John C. Thomas added colors matched to a box of 72 Crayola crayons [1][2]. The older values had been tuned for DEC VT240 terminals; Raveling retuned his on an HP monitor [8]. Dark slate grey was already in the list that shipped before 1989, at exactly today's 47, 79, 79, while plain slate grey arrived only with the 1989 expansion, so the dark one is the older of the two [8].

Early web browsers borrowed the X11 list, and the W3C later wrote it into SVG and CSS, adding a *grey* spelling beside every *gray* [1][3]. That is why `darkslategray` and `darkslategrey` both work today, and both mean #2F4F4F, red 47, green 79, blue 79 [3]. Paterson's dictionary of color lists it simply as one of the X11 colors [4].

sections.title: Why it looks odd
sections.body:
Its green and blue values are equal, so it leans toward teal, not blue [5]. Its supposed parent, `slategray` (#708090), is a lighter bluish grey, and the two sit about 23 units apart, with different hues [5]. The family names are a list of labels, not a system, and the web inherited worse: X11 *gray* was a light grey, while HTML's Gray was a mid grey, so in CSS `darkgray` is lighter than `gray` [1].

Its nearest relatives in older systems are Ridgway's [[greenish-slate-black]], the ISCC-NBS [[dusky-dull-bluish-green]] and the Japanese [[omeshicha]], all within three units [5]. Paterson defines slate grey simply as the color of grey slate, a dark grey [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The phrase is older than computers: *dark slate grey* appears in Google Books from the 1840s [6]. In our archive of 23,531 paintings, a color within six units of it covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 210, about as often in shadows as in mid-tones [7]. It is most loved by the Post-Impressionists: seven of Gauguin's fifty paintings in the archive carry it and six of Cézanne's, around fifteen times the archive's rate, and it often shares a canvas with [[petrol]] [7]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [7].
